newsitem.title: USA: Another Clinton question in U.S. funds controversy.
newsitem.headline: Another Clinton question in U.S. funds controversy.

text.p: One of the unanswered questions in the political fund-raising controversy dogging President Bill Clinton and his Democratic Party is whether Clinton himself solicited funds from a White House telephone.
This gained new attention on Tuesday after one of the congressional committees investigating the fund-raising uproar released documents suggesting he may have made such calls.

Clinton says he does not recall if he made calls or not, but has in any case stated he did nothing illegal in raising funds for his 1996 re-election effort and has defended similar calls made by Vice President Al Gore as legal if unwise.
Some critics claim such calls would break a law prohibiting partisan fund-raising on federal property. Others say the calls are wrong even in technically within the law.

"It's absolutely improper, without question," said Ellen Miller of the campaign finance watchdog group Public Campaign. "For the president to make these calls no matter where he called from is unethical, unacceptable and beyond the pale."
She said when the president of the United States asks for donations, it is almost impossible to turn him down. "The pressure is irresistable," she said.

Similarly, Bill Hogan, director of investigative projects at the Centre for Public Integrity, said "there is a question of propriety" in having a president solicit money, whether from the White House or not.

Documents released by the House of Representatives Government Oversight Committee show that Democratic Party officials suggested Clinton and Gore make calls in late 1995 to finance TV advertising for the 1996 presidential campaign.

Clinton and his party have been dogged for months by revelations of improper fund-raising tactics and the party's decision to return over $3 million to questionable donors, mainly with Asian-American business or government ties.
A Justice Department task force of 31 FBI agents, a Senate committee and the House panel are investigating.

One memo released by the House committee was addressed to former Deputy White House chief of staff Harold Ickes from former Democratic Party chairman Donald Fowler and others in the upper party echelon. It suggested Clinton make 18 to 20 calls and Gore make 10 calls as part of a campaign to raise an additional $4 million for the television ad campaign.
Former Clinton political advisor Dick Morris has credited the early television blitz with helping Clinton to beat Republican Bob Dole decisively in the November election.

Gore has admitted making phone calls from his White House office in 1995 and 1996 but said he never did "anything wrong, much less illegal." He said he used a Clinton-Gore campaign credit card and not taxpayer money.
Gore has nevertheless pledged never to do it again -- and his legalistic defence has sparked widespread ridicule.
But did Clinton make any such calls?
He has said he simply cannot remember, and the White House keeps reinforcing that position.
"The president said he didn't recall whether he did and I think that's where the matter stands," spokesman Mike McCurry said on Monday.
The document provided to House investigators was part of a series of papers that show the White House was kept fully informed of efforts to raise millions of dollars by the party.
They included dozens of White House coffees and other events attended by Clinton in 1995 and 1996, some aimed at raising as much as $400,000.
